chunks: "I'd use an H-bridge. It's four switches around the motor: two on the high side connecting to the supply and two on the low side to ground, with the motor across the middle.
Turn on the top-left and bottom-right and current flows one way through the motor; turn on top-right and bottom-left and it flows the other way.
Speed comes from PWM on one of the active switches.
The rules: never turn on both switches of the same leg, because that shorts the supply to ground, so there's a dead time between turning one off and the other on, and in a driver IC that's built in.
The body diodes of the FETs give the motor's inductive current a freewheel path when everything switches off.
With both low switches on I get braking; with all off the motor coasts.

From a microcontroller I'd normally drive it through an H-bridge IC or a gate driver with two inputs, either PWM plus a direction pin, or two inputs where each leg is driven separately, and the logic prevents the illegal state.
For the PWM I'd typically chop one switch while keeping the diagonal partner on, which gives lower ripple and good control.
If I only need occasional reversal at low speed, a DPDT relay does it, and if I have a split supply, a half-bridge with the motor to the middle point works too."
